Choose between two figures reported for the same line

Source: R/xbrl_resolve.R
xbrl_resolve.Rd

A filing sometimes states one statement line twice with different amounts. check_statement() refuses to pick and reports "conflicting duplicates", which leaves the statement unjudgeable. But the statement has to add up, and that is usually enough to decide: try each candidate, keep the reading that reconciles.

Usage

xbrl_resolve(x, by = c("basis", "period"), max_readings = 256L, tol = 1)

Arguments

x

A tibble from add_taxonomy().

by

Columns identifying one statement. Default c("basis", "period").

max_readings

Give up where the candidates multiply beyond this. Default 256.

tol

Absolute tolerance in the reporting currency. Default 1.

Value

x with the losing duplicates dropped and two columns added: resolved, TRUE on a line whose value this chose, and resolution, saying how – "rounding" where the figures were one number at two precisions, "empty context" where the rival figure was a nil column of its own, "arithmetic" where the sums decided. Lines with no conflict, and conflicts with no single best reading, come back untouched.

Most conflicts are rounding

Before any search, duplicates that differ only by rounding are collapsed. XBRL states the precision of every fact in its decimals attribute, so a filing that tags total assets as 1729466749 at decimals="0" and as 1729467000 at decimals="-3" has written one figure twice, not two figures. The exact one is kept.

One balance sheet, one context

Then the context. A balance sheet column is a single XBRL context – assets, equity and the liabilities all carry the same contextRef, because that is what a context is for. One filing in the corpus states its whole balance sheet twice: once in a context holding the figures, once in a context holding nothing but nils.

Neither a majority nor the arithmetic separates those two. The counts are equal, and an empty column adds up perfectly – nought is nought plus nought. What separates them is that a column of nils is not a statement, so the rule is kept to exactly that: a context whose every disputed figure is nil, where another has real ones, is an empty column and not a reading.

The same argument as find_signs()

find_signs() does not guess a sign; it enumerates the assignments and reports the one that reaches the total, or says there are several. This is the same search over a different unknown – not which sign a figure carries but which of two figures was meant – and it holds to the same rule. A conflict that admits one reconciling reading is resolved. One that admits several is left alone, because a statement that adds up two ways has not told us which way it meant.

Scoring

A candidate reading is scored by how many subtotals it settles: complete and sides agree count for it, sides differ and over-specified against. The winner must score above zero – a reading that settles nothing is not a resolution – and must beat every other outright.

Ties are left unresolved. Over the corpus, breaking them by taking the first best reading settled seven conflicts, and the picks were visibly wrong: nil for one company's short-term debt, and a figure for another's total assets that was neither of the two under dispute. Eight of the fifteen had a single best reading, and those are the ones worth having.

What this cannot do

It resolves a conflict; it does not diagnose one. Where a filer has used one element for two different things – gross and net deferred tax, say – the arithmetic picks whichever fits the statement, which is the right figure for the balance sheet and says nothing about why the other is there.

See also

check_statement(), which reports the conflict, and xbrl_fill(), which derives what is absent rather than choosing between what is present.

Other taxonomy: add_taxonomy(), check_breakdown(), check_cascade(), check_cashflow(), check_continuity(), check_inclusion(), check_movement(), check_statement(), read_taxonomy(), xbrl_accounts(), xbrl_company(), xbrl_fill(), xbrl_lines(), xbrl_movements(), xbrl_note_tables(), xbrl_panel(), xbrl_period(), xbrl_ratios(), xbrl_report(), xbrl_report_data(), xbrl_robustness(), xbrl_screen(), xbrl_standardise(), xbrl_validate()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
x <- read_xbrl("13645183_2024-12-31.xml")
check_statement(x)$verdict                  # "conflicting duplicates"
check_statement(xbrl_resolve(x))$verdict    # "complete"
} # }
